review_text_raw:
Mainlining is a nifty little adventure game with a hacking theme that, unlike other hacking games available on steam, eschews the nitty gritty of command-line interface wizardry in favor of telling a succint story well within its means.  That is to say, if you've avoided other hacking games because they emulate real-world operating systems all too closely, you can relax - Mainlining's CLI is quite simple and doesn't require any foreknowledge of how command-line operating systems work.

Instead of bringing the hardcore keyboard thunder, Mainlining opts for funtional aesthetics.  When you first start up the game, you'll be looking at a pixelated mock-up of a WinXP-like desktop.  Though typing away in the CLI is a big part of the game, you'll only ever need three or four commands, all of which are easy to remember.  The rest is as you would normally navigate a desktop OS these days - with a mouse.  Throughout the game, you will load applications onto your start bar, read files on your desktop notepad, and browse a well-realized fake web, all the while using information you find to remotely hack into other systems.  Throughout several cases, you will follow a bread-crumb trail that will eventually unravel to reveal a story.

That story being you work for MI7, a sister org to the famous MI5, only its main focus is online activity facilitating real-world crimes, and the backdrop of all this is a new act simply called the BLU Pill.  While it never gets into specifics, BLU Pill basically enables the gov't to break into systems legally in order to fight crime.  Naturally, this angers a few people and they organize themselves into a secret hacking group to counter MI7's efforts.  The game makes no hard stance on the politics of such a law, but throughout the game, you're never quite sure if you're the good guy or the bad guy.

In any case, this is all handled with beautiful pixel-style art from end-to-end, from presenting you nostalgic mock-ups of popular desktops (WinXP, iOS, etc) to a whole database full of pixel faces of the citizens of wherever you are.  In terms of aesthetics, Mainlining really reminded me of Digital A Love Story, and it unfolds in a very similar manner.  As you read chat logs and other random files you nab off unsuspecting systems, you'll learn about the inhabitants of this world and the characters found therein.  Moreover, there are live chat windows on your screen that dole out large portions of the story and all you ever have are names.  You're not told who's who, but it eventually all slots into place.

While I didn't encounter any glaring bugs, the game doesn't give you a lot of options to go off-script, nor does it make any effort throw any red herrings at you so unless you're really trying to find ways to break the game, you likely won't have a problem.  At all times, I was patienly waiting for the proverbial Other Shoe, but it never really came.  As each day/case passes, you'll be told what you need to find in order to proceed and any previously-learned knowledge usually doesn't work again, so going off the beaten path doesn't really present itself.  You either figure out what to do next or you don't.

That being said, I completed the game in about 2 hours or so and never even so much as wished for a hint.  All of the challenges in the game are easily met and good segments of the game are just waiting around for some things to happen.  I can't really describe more since that would spoil it, but for the most part, it plays a lot like the old standard of cutscene -> gameplay -> cutscene.

All in all, I found Mainlining to be an enjoyable experience and a perfect entry point into the genre since it really does a little of everything.  Outside of some proofreading mishaps, the game is solid.

review_text_raw:
TL:DR; Good game, short and to the point. Sometimes too easy but worth a buy, especially if found on sale.

Pros: 
-Great Artstyle (If you like Papers, Please or Please Don't Touch Anything you will love this)
-Great Gameplay Ideas (would love to see other game with that Switching OS's idea)
-Later Half of the game does a good job of switching things up on you and making the situation feel a bit more personal
-The Mainline system did make me feel a bit badass at times (Possible a con for some, since the gameplay for it don't change at all through out the game, i was ok with it)

Cons:
-Game is too linear, just when you think you can explore a bit just for fun. You find out the devs never programmed anything that far. (Example: You might find a website or email address, and you want to look it up just for fun but the devs never made anything for it. Would be nice to have more side stuff to hack into or mess around with.)
-Difficulty to some might be level of hand holding
-You personally never feel really attached to anything as a player and the character you play as (You don't really feel like you or your character is a part of the world and everything going on in it, the later chapters start to sort of fix that but by the time you feel something the game is over.)
-Like i said in the Pros list the Mainline System is the main gameplay aspect used in this game (To hack, check IP address, download stuff, etc.) and it can get repetative since it does not change at all


 This was my first foray in the Hacker-esque type of games. I had my eye on Orwell, Uplink, Hacknet, etc. but Mainlining hit the right spot with its artwork reminding me of Papers, Please (there might be people that hate that fact that so many games are in a sense "copying" that style but to me i can get enough of it, if done right). 

 Took me about 8 hours to beat but honestly i left the computer running during gameplay many times so i would say a leisure run through this game for me was really about 6 hours. Once over the game definitely leaves you wanting more but the aesthetics of the "papers' please" type of games always has that to it (Perfect example is the great game "Please Don't Touch Anything").

 Difficulty was honestly easy, very easy, sometimes holding your hand easy...but for my first outing in this type of game it showed me what was possible with it and left me wanting a game developer to take advantage of it, so to say in short i kinda have a hunger for more games like this but I definitely need more challenge.

 Gameplay mechanics and story was very well done, for a kickstarted game. It seems like the devs had a plan they wanted to execute, they just needed money and once they got the support they needed, they created it flawlessly. The only downside to that is the game feels very linear (Meaning i wish there was even more stuff i could hack it to just for fun, other peoples emails, websites, etc. there's to little in this playground of a gameworld once you really get into it.) but like i said its a kickstarter game so i have forgiveness for it, if it was otherwise i would have to say i feel like the game devs didn't want to strive for more and just wanted to create the bare minimum needed to call it a finished project.

All in all, good game, short and to the point. Worth a buy, especially if found on sale like i did.

review_text_raw:
Mainlining is a cyberpunk-inspired investigative adventure that turns the ordinary process of browsing files, reading emails, and searching databases into a tense and immersive detective experience. Developed by Rebelephant and published by Merge Games, the game places players behind the screen of a government intelligence computer system where every clue, suspect, and secret must be uncovered through hacking, surveillance, and careful analysis of digital information. Instead of relying on action sequences or cinematic set pieces, Mainlining builds suspense entirely through deduction, atmosphere, and the unsettling realization that every citizen’s private life is only a few clicks away from exposure.

The game is set in a near-future Britain where privacy laws have collapsed following the introduction of the BLU Pill Act, legislation that grants intelligence agencies unrestricted access to personal digital information. Players take on the role of an operative working for MI7, a government surveillance division tasked with tracking cybercriminals after a major breach compromises national security. What initially appears to be a series of disconnected investigations slowly evolves into a larger conspiracy involving corruption, abuse of power, political manipulation, and the dangers of mass surveillance. The story feels particularly effective because its themes mirror real-world debates surrounding government monitoring and digital privacy, giving the experience a level of relevance that extends beyond simple science fiction.

One of Mainlining’s greatest achievements is its presentation. The entire game takes place inside a simulated retro computer operating system inspired by older versions of Windows desktops. Every action occurs through email clients, command prompts, browsers, folders, chat programs, and intelligence databases, creating the illusion that the player is genuinely operating inside a classified surveillance network. This design choice immediately establishes immersion because players interact with the world exactly the way an investigator would. The retro-inspired pixel art and low-tech interface also contribute heavily to the atmosphere, giving the game a gritty and believable cyberpunk identity without relying on flashy visuals.

Gameplay revolves around investigating suspects by hacking into personal computers and analyzing digital traces left behind in their online activity. Players search through conversations, photographs, browsing histories, financial records, and social media interactions in order to uncover evidence and identify criminal behavior. Unlike many detective games that heavily guide the player toward obvious solutions, Mainlining encourages independent thinking and observation. Important clues are often hidden within seemingly unimportant files or casual conversations, forcing players to pay close attention to details instead of simply following objective markers.

The command-line hacking mechanics are surprisingly immersive despite their simplicity. Players use text commands to access networks, trace IP addresses, and infiltrate systems, creating the feeling of performing real investigative work without becoming inaccessible to newcomers. The game succeeds because it understands how to make information itself feel rewarding. Discovering a hidden message, uncovering an encrypted file, or linking multiple suspects together creates genuine excitement because progress depends entirely on the player’s own deductions rather than scripted sequences.

What truly separates Mainlining from other hacking-themed games is the moral discomfort that develops over time. Although the player technically works for law enforcement, many of the investigative methods feel invasive and ethically questionable. Reading intimate personal conversations, examining private photographs, and monitoring every aspect of someone’s digital life creates a constant sense of unease. The game repeatedly raises questions about whether unrestricted surveillance can ever remain justified once governments gain the ability to observe every citizen without limitations. Even when tracking criminals, the player often feels disturbingly close to violating the boundaries of innocent people.

The investigations themselves remain varied enough to keep the campaign engaging. Cases involve cybercrime, hacking groups, drug operations, financial fraud, and organized conspiracies that slowly reveal deeper connections hidden beneath the surface. Players must carefully identify suspects, gather evidence, and determine physical locations before making arrests. Wrong accusations can result in failure, adding pressure to every investigation and encouraging players to double-check conclusions before acting. This structure creates a satisfying detective experience because success feels earned through careful reasoning rather than random guessing.

The writing throughout the game is consistently strong. Dialogue balances serious political themes with dry humor and believable character interactions that prevent the experience from becoming overly bleak. Emails, online chats, and casual conversations reveal small personality details that make suspects and supporting characters feel authentic despite the minimalist presentation. The game gradually builds a believable world where political fear, digital dependence, and government overreach have become deeply intertwined with everyday life.

The soundtrack complements the atmosphere exceptionally well. Electronic music and ambient background tracks create a constant feeling of tension and paranoia without overwhelming the quieter investigative moments. Combined with the glowing retro desktop aesthetic and endless streams of digital information, the audio design reinforces the sense that players are trapped inside a cold and impersonal surveillance system.

Despite its originality, Mainlining is not completely free from flaws. Some investigations can become repetitive because the gameplay loop often revolves around similar patterns of searching files and tracing connections. Certain clues are occasionally too obscure, leading to moments where progression slows due to unclear objectives. The command-line interface, while immersive, can also feel awkward at times because typing errors or unclear system responses occasionally interrupt the pacing. Players expecting action-heavy hacking gameplay may also find the experience too slow because most of the tension comes from reading, analyzing information, and making logical deductions rather than participating in high-energy sequences.

The visual presentation, while stylish, is intentionally minimalistic and may not appeal to everyone. Those expecting large cinematic environments or highly animated storytelling may initially find the desktop-only structure limiting. However, the simplicity ultimately becomes one of the game’s strengths because it keeps the player fully focused on the investigation itself rather than external distractions.

Although it lacks major production values or complex action mechanics, Mainlining stands out as one of the more memorable indie hacking adventures available. Its investigative gameplay, morally ambiguous storytelling, and immersive interface design create a unique experience that rewards patience, observation, and curiosity. Players interested in conspiracy thrillers, cybercrime investigations, and narrative-driven puzzle games will likely find themselves completely absorbed by its dark digital world.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw: Honestly I wanted to like this, but there's just too many irritating bad things about everything from story to design. It takes place in a city so fictional that it's hard to care about it - it exists only because it needs to have a game be set in it. From the technology perspective nothing makes sense. Especially if you work in anything related to IT, it will simply make you cringe. You hack into people's computers simply by finding their IP address... It's like you're living inside a meme. The interface tries to resemble Windows XP for some reason... Even though the game is very low res pixelated, which makes no sense. Nothing is visually pleasant or cool to interact with. Everything inside is barely functional jank, like the notepad that doesn't let you save files or move the cursor into previously entered lines. Honestly, Steam's notes or even pen & paper are more useful, so it's hard to say why this exists. The method of investigating cases is repetitive and boring and a lot has to be based on guesswork, detaching the game from it's intelligence gathering theme. Even worse is how you solve them, which is simply a blind test that you can repeat infinitely until you get all the elements right. It's just disappointing, after playing Uplink and Hypnospace Outlaw there's really nothing that would make me consider going back to Mainlining even for a moment.

This game has three elements I really like in games:

The "hacking" part, although it's very simple (hacknet, uplink etc)
The point and click game puzzle genre
an overarching story that could be interesting

So this SHOULD have been a big win for me. And yet, I had more annoyance going through the first 6 cases than fun. And that's all due to... the gameplay. 

You could ask yourself how. To summarize:
- an alternative system/desktop with some kind of mandala thing going on that'll make you dizzy if you look at it too much
- Constant chatting noises, distracting you easely from whatever path you were following. In the first few cases it's not too bad, but the BOOP BOOP BOOP continuous sound makes you mad
- Meanwhile you're trying to concentrate on the puzzles, but shit is happening at the same time, so you have to be fast. Or at least that's what the game seemingly pushes you to do. But the joy of a point and click is discovering options until you find something that clicks

It's not a hard game but the way it's build makes it unplayable, for me. I saw this comes from an old Bundlestars/Fanatical bundle that has some killer games alongside it, but this one ain't it. I'm glad I gave up, this was more stressful than working a real detective job (I'd imagine)

review_text_raw:
Pretty boring, to be honest. It feels so much like a bootleg version of Hacknet, except without the badass soundtracks and cool hacking features.


[b]/STORY and CHARACTERS (6/10)/[/b]

First things first, let's start with the story and characters. You're an agent from the government cyber security agency MI7 that investigates with other MI7 agents a group of hackers called Thorn who breached their servers. Your job is to track down all the members of the group and arrest them for a different crime in order to hide the security breach to the public. Alright, sounds simple enough, but that's because it IS simple, it's not more fleshed out than that. You spend the whole game hunting down an entire hacker group, then find an excuse to arrest them (I'll get back on that later). Even when you detain the big leader, none of what you've done felt satisfying after that.

As for the characters, well you don't have that much of character development from them, except for the "smart girl of the team" agent Sharp, the "bossy boss who takes his job way too seriously" Osvalt, the "I prefer old TTS softwares" agent on the field Cooper, the "flirty secretary who puts winky emojis all over her emails" Ashley, the "hahaha, I'm evil" hacker group leader Mr. Blue. Anyway, you get the point. Each character is only limited to one main characteristic and that's it.

[b]/GAMEPLAY (4/10)/[/b]

Oh boy, the gameplay is the main(lining) reason why I'm not recommending this. Jeez, where do I start? Well, first of all, if you're expecting to feel like a hacker, you're in for a disappointment. All you get is a command-prompt application with two script-kiddie commands: one that gets a website's IP and one that hacks into someone's computer using the said IP. That's right, throughout the whole game you'll spend most of your time typing 'ping', 'iphack', 'ping', 'iphack' while searching a computer's files in a DOS-style file navigation system. The devs claimed that it was on purpose in order to emphasize the narration over actual hacking. I would be fine with that kind of decision, but that doesn't mean you should stick to that repetitive "look at a website, ping, iphack and read files" bulls hit. At least keep an enjoyable gameplay in the background as well. Luckily, you get some other apps (like the google map one) and Operating Systems on the way.

On top of that, the arrest system is really nitpicky about which evidence you use against the person. Each case has around three alternate crimes to choose from to arrest the person you're tracking. Summary: The story was pretty good, and has other things going for it, but it feels really unpolished, poor UI, typos etc.

Things I did like: The story was engaging, and the writers did a good job in making their points about government surveillance. The core hacking gameplay is also good (albeit not very realistic but this is at least explained in game). They did a good job theming the OSes.

Things I didn't like: The UI is not good, I get that they aren't going to recode in a whole desktop environment, but you can't resize windows, text files that are opened cannot be minimized nor do they show up in the taskbar. This makes windows all overlap in an annoying way. The other thing I didn't like is the lack of continuity between cases. Changing the IP addresses each case is annoying. The fact I couldn't take more than like 256 characters of notes in the notepad app is also annoying. You can't move your cursor back to insert something into text, you have to delete it and start over.

Its weird the game's narrative and the story cases all link together but the gamestate basically wipes at each case. For example I would have liked to keep a list of websites I visited, as well as persons of interest and details about each. But because the notes are all deleted from case to case (in fact they are deleted as soon as you close the notepad app). It makes that pointless. Files are the same way, all your downloaded files are deleted from case to case. Sometimes in a detective game its useful to go back to reference old info, even if its not immediately useful for solving the case. I just felt that the game's mechanics kept holding me back from being fully immersed in the game.

There are also alot of typos. Some of which are in important places.

The way you turn in cases is also kinda clunky. Its a good idea but it ends up being frustrated on several cases. There is also not any rewards or effects on the story for getting the highest rating for cases.

review_text_raw:
Thoroughly enjoyed this game from start to finish - i've never actually enjoyed point-and-click adventures before, but the whole premace of this one caught my eye, and I'm glad it did!

The positives are that its great fun, makes you feel like you could go out and hack the white house, and you actually build up a mental rapport on various people throughout the story - by the final mission just seeing certain names that cropped up elsewhere was enough to push me in the right direction. There-in lies another positive: the game, despite being a point-and-click, has enough 'flesh' in non-important things to allow you to wonder off what you are supposed to be doing, something that I think is often not done in similar games of the genre, and is the reason i dont normally enjoy point-and-clicks.

Amongst other things, the other great positives to this game, in my opinion, is the humor centred around parodying real life, which is not only present in the main story line, but also in areas 'around' it (by which i mean in the file systems of people unrelated to your mission, etc)

The downsides? I sometimes felt as though I was just guessing at what files might be incriminating, and even when i succeeded i occasionally didnt really understand why. The second downside is the fact that I have finished the game in it's current state (7 missions) in juyst 2.5 hours. I mess around a lot, so someone who was really trying and understood everything about the game could probably be doine with it in under 2 hours. Secondly, I dont see much replay value in it - however, i dont usually see replay value in many things so this could just be me.

Overall I do think that this game is worth the money - not only this but the game will soon have a further 6 (or something around that i think) missions added on in early February. I think that if you are reading this and dont know whether to buy or not, just go and get the demo - the missions in that aren't actually directly related to the missions in the full game, so you will get a good idea of what it is like without having to replay parts upon purchasing

Also, the windows XP nostalgia by itself was worth it!

review_text_raw:
It may be worth waiting for a sale on this one, but it isn't actually bad.

Allegedly inspired by real life privacy laws being passed in England, Mainlining is a government hacking game where you play as a member of the mysterious agency MI7, aka the "Lions". It's okay though, you're the lightly comedy kind of oppressive government. You've even got an agent who exists entirely to be a walking Twin Peaks reference. Ha ha.

You're allowed via the "BLU Pill Act" to hack into any PC you want, but you can only arrest people if you can produce evidence towards one of three charges: Selling illegal items (5 years), Theft of data or physical items (10 years), or the most heinous, life-destroying crime of all... Unlicensed Software Development (25 years).

The anti-government activist group THORNS however is working on counter-hacking the hackers. Can you capture them before...

...well, nothing actually really happens, because here's the thing: Mainlining is way less a hacking game and more of a traditional point and click adventure. If there's a way to game over, I didn't find it, and I tried things like arresting random people out of the phone book a half-dozen times just to see if the newspaper articles accusing MI7 of being incompetent losers ever got more fed up. (They did not.)

So in practice the tiers of arrest serve as self-imposed difficulty levels for the most part. Poke around a little, find someone selling drugs, arrest them for 5. Or you can poke further, discover they're being framed and arrest the framer for a data violation. Or you can push further and arrest the guy who wrote the software that made it possible for the framer to do his work.

There's no branching plotlines based on who you arrest, you just kind of bomf along to the next case.

I went out of my way to investigate everything and finished this in about four hours, so it's not going to strain anybody. However, it's because I went out of my way to investigate everything that I'm not sure I can rec this one very hard.

By the end of the game the typos are out of control (including in MISSION CRITICAL places, which ought to be a showstopper right there), the plot makes less and less sense, and more and more sites are introduced that you SHOULD be able to hack but can't. You'll have a great idea about where to look next and ... oops, no, that site mentioned in an email doesn't actually exist. 

I spent a fair amount of time towards the endgame going "Oh. Well that should've worked though?" and that's never something you want people saying about your adventure game. I feel like there was a big scope in mind and they had to cut it down and cut it back for actual release.

Mainlining has a lot of cute ideas about the hacking genre, and it's not a total wash of a game. It's just flawed, and you really really have to know that going in.

This was a fun game to play with a decent story that kept me engaged. All the "puzzles" consist of information gathering by following the paper trail via hacking to various computers and arresting suspects with the right evidence. The game is broken up into individual "chapters" which each ending once an arrest is made. The chapters have an overarching story but some also feel slightly independent in terms of the focus for each, which was a very nice blend in how the story was developed. The graphics and sound were great, as well the user interface which cleverly worked well. 

The only complaints that I have about the game were some glitches toward the end of it, but nothing that prevented me from enjoying/finishing the game. I encountered some minor glitches such as particular scrollbars that don't work with the mouse wheel, folders that were mutually exclusive to being shown, scrollbars for unrelated windows that worked in unison, window bleed-through with the map, close buttons that were off-centered from the correct position on a window, etc. It almost felt like they ran out of time to do some technical polishing/hardening toward the end since a lot of the issues seemed obvious.

I truly wanted to recommend this game because it has got so many things nicely done. Cute pixel art and simulated websites, dialogues between agents, decent story, amusing chat logs, good writing, moving from one clue to another, arresting someone each day... It isn't exactly a hacking simulation but that it isn't a big issue for me either. I played a lot of hacking simulation games and when I realized this isn't exactly one of them (hacking in this is all about typing only a handful console commands) I didn't care much, doing some simple detective work and enjoying it as if a visual novel could also be enough for me. 

Firstly, the game is a little buggy and sometimes crashes, I think it crashed 4 times during my playthrough, so I had to start a case from scratch while almost at the point of moving next one, because game autosaves only at the start of a new case. 

The real annoying problem with this game is the 'evidence' part. It is pretty simple. You download a lot of files, find the real names of the devious anti-government hackers who all have nicknames, then find really incriminating documents about them, then you attempt to arrest them using the very obvious document you have seized... but it doesn't work. The game says, with a newspaper article after your attempted to arrest, that the security service you work for has wrongly accused an innocent person. The document, although even the most incriminating one, blatantly mentioning everything about the hacker, his real name and activities is somehow the wrong document... Instead, it is one of the other documents with containing a lot less information, sometimes even not containing any information related to the case. So after awhile you give up, get extremely bored and simply go from file to file, trying each one of them to arrest the suspect and one of them works because devs decided only one of them should work even though there is not a concrete reason why only that one should work. I finished the game, but it was a througly annoying experience. I don't think I could have finished it if the game didn't have such good writing and story.

There are much better hacking simulation games out there, even if you have played all of them, I still recommend skipping this one because it doesn't award the time you spent on going through all those documents. Really badly designed, I don't what they were thinking.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR (good deal of gameplay from free demo):  Mainlining is a fun adventure game with a clever and unique twist where you hack computers, websites, and other devices to mine information on the different cases presented to you.  The game doesn't hold your hand, so the cases can present a fun little challenge beyond the first tutorial.  Highly recommended!  If you want to see a playthrough of the first (tutorial) case, check out this video (Demo version):

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kek4zO0OF_8

FULL REVIEW:  Mainlining, the point-and-click hacking adventure game, casts the player as an employee of MI7 in charge of investigating various cyber-crimes and tracking suspects through electronic means.  You are given tools (e.g., electronic trackers, a simplified command-line, web browser, etc) in order to collect information, put together clues, and ultimately arrest the right person.

There is a lot of unique gameplay in Mainlining since, unlike other adventure games, the puzzles and stories you try to untangle are pieced together from short emails, blog posts, and other electronic files.  The game does a good job of not holding your hand (e.g., by telling you which sites to hack, etc) but does provide sufficient in-context clues so that the task isn’t impossible and/or a guessing game. I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Mainlining is a story-driven hacking-flavoured thriller/adventure game with gameplay closer to a point-and-click adventure than than the "Hollywood" hackers (Uplink, etc).

Set in a slightly dystopian near future, you are an MI7 agent empowered to hack into citizen's computers to prevent cybercrime.  Each chapter presents the player with a new crime to solve by finding IPs, connecting to them, downloading documents, and following the trail until you can apply for an arrest warrant.

Graphics and sound are all serviceable, characters dialogue are charming, and the developers put a lot of time into huge suspect database, variety of interfaces, and multiple solutions to each chapter.

Mainlining is solid game from a small indie team, but does lack polish in a few areas. A number of websites that should exist in the game do not, there are numerous spelling errors and several "Welcome, $USERNAME" type bugs, and the in-game tools have a lot of minor UX issues that can be frustrating.  In particular, the warrant system is somewhat notorious for being too exacting, but the cost of failure is low, so it is tolerable.

Overall definitely worth a playthough if you like the demo.

Well, I like the idea of the game and I found its story somewhat enjoyable. There are many nods to actual existing software. But even when I knew exactly what I had to do, I sometimes just looked into a walkthrough to spare myself from having to go through all the annoying gameplay mechanics again. Instead of repeating what other people have already said, let me first point you to two well-written negative reviews that pinpoint exactly what made the gameplay kind of a chore:

https://steamcommunity.com/id/algorithman/recommended/454950/

https://steamcommunity.com/id/Oloko0/recommended/454950/

In addition to that, the concept of the missions is sometimes weird. Every mission ends by arresting a single suspect. Sometimes you just have 1 suspect, sometimes there are 3 possible suspects and you just have to arrest any of them, not all 3. That's also the case in a mission where you're just told to find information on a person who went missing years ago. You can randomly find information on her ex-husband, arrest him for producing drugs with her, and you win. And the game just never even follows up on that, except in the credits where you suddenly find out that the missing person is dead.

There's other weird stuff going on like a puzzle in the final mission where you need to find the suspect's son's first name, and in the ending, he suddenly has a different name. I also found a placeholder document that said something like "Following the suspect's arrest on [date the player arrested him]"

Mainlining is much more of a point-and-click thriller with an annoying interface rather than a hacking game, but I did not expect a simulation anyway. You can finish it in 4 hours and I kinda enjoyed it for the most part, but it's super unpolished and vague and the devs never bothered releasing an update. I wouldn't buy it unless it's heavily discounted.

Out of all those hacking and investigation games like Hacknet, Hacker Evolution, Orwell, The Black Watchmen, and Hypnospace Outlaw, this is the one you can skip.

[h1] Neutral Recommendation: Only Pick Up At A Discount [/h1]

- [b]Gameplay:[/b]  Interfacing with the game is fairly straightforward. You're using a simulation of a computer desktop. The main complaint is that you can only backspace to make changes to text in the Notepad program. You cannot edit the text freely, so if you want to make a change to something at the top of the file, you'd have to erase everything and start over. Luckily, you'll find that program is mostly useless.

The lame thing is that, for most cases, you can only turn in one-piece of evidence linking the person to the crime, although there may be several in reality. Also, you have to pick the right location for the person, so even if you have the evidence correct, if you don't choose the right location, it somehow ends up as a False Arrest. It doesn't really make any sense that you could have sufficient evidence, but a person is [i][b]Falsely Accused[/b][/i] because they were in a different location than you originally thought they were (i.e. at work instead of at home.) That's just dumb...

- [b]Plot/Story:[/b]  This is also fairly straightforward and not very awe-inspiring. You're working for a Big Brother goverment agency that was hacked and it's your job to bring down the Cyber Terrorists in fine fashion. The story is mostly told through Emails and Documents you find while hacking systems. It is honestly pretty forgettable, and is not very long.

- [b]Graphics:[/b]  This is a very minimalist retro-style game. The text takes a bit to get used to reading, in its pixelated format. There are no actual graphics options for tuning the look of the game.

- [b]Music:[/b]  The soundtrack is actually decent for this type of game. It's nothing to shake a stick at, but was mostly just chill music to give a spy-ish undertone to the game.

- [b]Overall:[/b]  I give the game a [b]6.5/10[/b]. It's fairly short, and was kind of interesting to play through, but it is an utterly forgettable experience that will leave you wanting to play something similar, but with much better design. Also... you will come to hate the chime sound every time you get a new chat or email.

review_text_raw:
A good game, but could use some polish to become a great one.

Let me start with a pro/con list so you don't have to sift through my personal thoughts in longform.

Pros:
-Doesn't hold your hand, feels 'authentic'. You feel like you're hacking, in some small way.
-Satisfying UI, easy to navigate without tutorial.
-Challenging without being mind-bendingly difficult or frustrating (usually).
-Interesting story with fun twists and turns and a lot of personal flourish to make it feel alive.
-Offers several solutions to almost every case, the result is up to what you turn in.
-Good music and ambient sound.
Cons:
-Bit of a buggy mess sometimes. Had to reset several cases when things stopped working, and had the entire game freeze at one point.
-Doesn't do much to make you feel "involved" in the story...you are a silent and non-engaging protagonist. Things happen to you and around you, you do not really interact except hacking.
-A few times, it suffers from "Figure out what the devs were thinking" syndrome.
-Lots of typos and a few places where things were not implemented but were left in the script for players to see

Mainlining is a good game with a lot of potential. I love the concept of an adventure game told through hacking and desktop UIs. But it really needs a good strong polish to truly be a satisfying experience. It's a short, light-hearted bit of fun, which I enjoyed! Don't expect a deep hacking experience like Uplink...this is primarily an adventure game. However, the narrative was too short and not engaging enough for me to really feel totally sucked in or invested....exciting things lose their emphasis because it's all told to you the same way with very little pause for breath or impact, or it happens "off screen".

However, I think this game is fun, interesting, unique and worth a play for sure. I found it easy to forgive its little hiccups and lack of polish because I was so charmed by Mainlining. If you enjoy feeling like a hacker, government intrigue, solving mysteries and adventure games, I think you will really find something to like here.

The basic idea of the game is really cool, but the amount of bug and bad UI design makes it really unpleasant to play.

Placeholders in the text

Story bugging and not letting you progress so you need to restart the whole mission from scratch
Game settings not working (fullscreen setting not being applied correctly)
Game not playing sound

I really was enjoying the game at first, but after a few level it just became really anoying to play.

Mainlining is a game that is generally worth a try, even though it is pretty simple to beat and quite short (I spent 4.3 hours beating the game). The gaming time vs price ratio is therefore average at best, with no replay potential. 

About the games, contrary to other reviewers I have not been annoyed by bugs. The plot is nice even though it gets sometimes confusing, which is probably something the devs wanted. 
The thrill of discovering things in someone else's computer is nice but unfortunately there is little things that have absolutely no link to the story. It is disappointing that everything seems to have a purpose. I don't believe that the same should be filled with dozen of useless files but it would have be interesting to have some sorting to do between the useless stuff and the stuff that is actually useful. This makes you feel that you are just pulling a string that leads you to the end. There is very little occasions where you actually have to think to get through the case. For example I am very disappointed that there is no decryption challenges (hidden in pictures, fileinfo, enigma...)

The arrest system is badly designed as you have to use exactly the good file and therefore make a lot of false arrest that have by the way absolutely no consequences. 

So the game is a generally good experience and it is enjoyable to go through the story, but the whole thing is only dedicated to the story and this lack of content does not serve the game's potential...

"Unique" is a great word to describe Mainlining, there's nothing quite like it out there. At its heart, the game is a point and click adventure. The subject matter surrounds techno-ethics and hacking. The story is very well written and the game works hard to immerse the player into a parallel world set in the shady corners of 2010's internet. 

Graphically the game uses cool pixel art and the soundtrack complements the game perfectly without ever getting in the way. There are a number of different outcomes to each case which offers some level of replayability. I encountered on or two glitches and bugs but the game’s lone developer is working hard to fix these as they pop up. 

I’ve enjoyed Mainlining a lot. It’s like reading a good book, full of twists and turns and a large spoonful of humour.

- Could be more of a choose your own adventure

Now there are more cons than pros I will admit that but they're small cons that are just me being picky.  I still highly recommend it.

review_text_raw:
I have been teetering on the recommendation for Mainlining for quite a while, and I think I'd recommend this game only to fans of detective and/or hacking sims, or if you can grab it on a sale. 

The game features good art, great music and I really enjoyed the pixelated re-imagination of multiple operating-systems, albeit the pixel-fonts are a little hard to read at times. 
Generally speaking, I think Mainlining is more of a detective than hacking simulation. The hacking aspect is relatively simplistic and the game's limited command line turns hacking into a bit of a chore, i.e. you are required to type the same set of commands over and over for every new case and history or tab-completion isn't supported. At least, you are able to abbreviate most commands to their initial, e.g. "a", instead of typing out the entire commend. I find it puzzling, that possibility of abbreviating commands (that doesn't exist in a RL command line) wasn't communicated in the game itself, rather I stumbled upon this in a video-review. Nonetheless, I did enjoy playing this game at a virtual computer screen, and each case created enough suspension to keep me interested until the ending credits rolled.

While I have fond memories of the OS environments, my overall enjoyment of the game got hampered by frequent and annoying bugs as well as seemingly careless typos. Furthermore, these issues increase in frequency and the game is noticeably decreasing in quality in the latter half.
